lesson_title: The 400 000 Volt Journey to Your Plug
hook_text: The electricity in your plug may have travelled at 400 000 volts to reach you. Why so high?
clip_script: Your electricity probably began hundreds of kilometres away, at a power station in Mpumalanga. A step-up transformer pushed its voltage to about 400 000 volts, and it raced across the country on tall steel pylons. Why so high? Power is voltage times current. Carry 100 megawatts at 400 000 volts and you need only 250 amperes. Drop to 20 000 volts and you need 5 000 amperes, twenty times more current, and the wires would waste about four hundred times more energy as heat. Near your town, substations step the voltage down, and a transformer on a pole or in a green box in your street brings it to 230 volts. And all of it must balance: when demand is bigger than supply, areas are switched off in turns, load shedding, to save the grid.
visual_style: Pylons marching across the Highveld; a transformer animation with coils; glowing wires comparing two currents; a map of the grid with an evening demand curve rising.
pacing: Question open, a fast journey down the voltage ladder, a pause on the calculation, a firm close on balance.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and spot the transformer nearest your home.
